claims.text: The starting materials are crystalline, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles composed of five or more metals.
Tungsten and molybdenum are refractory metals suitable as the proposed minor alloying addition.
Adding a minor amount of tungsten or molybdenum can overcome structural or chemical instability in the nanoparticles.
The proposed stabilization applies during operation from 773 to 1173 K for hours to days.
The introduced refractory-metal atoms act as stabilizers.
The refractory-metal addition reduces atomic diffusion rates.
The refractory-metal addition suppresses defect formation.
Reduced diffusion and suppressed defect formation preserve nanoparticle structural stability.
Reduced diffusion and suppressed defect formation preserve nanoparticle chemical stability.
Refractory-metal-modified nanoparticles will be more stable than otherwise identical nanoparticles without the addition.
Refractory-metal-modified nanoparticles will have better catalytic performance than otherwise identical nanoparticles without the addition.
Approximately equimolar compositions are characteristic of high-entropy alloys containing five or more metallic elements.
X-ray diffraction, transmission electron microscopy, and energy-dispersive spectroscopy can be used to assess structural and chemical changes.
A lack of improved catalytic performance relative to the unmodified control would falsify the hypothesis.
Significant structural or chemical instability in the refractory-metal-modified nanoparticles would falsify the hypothesis.
